question_text:
Archaeologists often compare how heavily different parts of a landscape were used in the past by measuring how many artifacts turn up in a standard amount of excavated ground. A team surveying an ancient farming region recovered fragments of broken pottery, called sherds, from four sites. Each site was dug in 1-meter-by-1-meter units, but the team excavated a different number of units at each site because of differences in access and soil depth. The lead archaeologist hypothesized that the ancient farmers discarded pottery more densely at sites on the river terrace than at sites on the hillside.

Which choice best describes data from the table that support the archaeologist's hypothesis?
answer_a: Each river terrace site had fewer excavated units than each hillside site.
answer_b: Each river terrace site recovered more sherds per excavated unit than either hillside site did.
answer_c: The two hillside sites together recovered more sherds than the two river terrace sites combined.
answer_d: Both river terrace sites recovered more sherds than the hillside site Dunmore Ridge did.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it describes a comparison that supports the hypothesis that pottery was discarded more densely at river terrace sites. Because the team excavated different numbers of units at each site, density has to be judged by sherds recovered per excavated unit, not by raw totals. Dividing each site's sherds by its units gives 40 for Alder Flat (480 / 12) and 35 for Cedar Bend (700 / 20) on the river terrace, compared with 28 for Birch Knoll (840 / 30) and 26 for Dunmore Ridge (650 / 25) on the hillside. The lowest river terrace value is therefore higher than the highest hillside value.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. Although the table does show that the river terrace sites (12 and 20 units) had fewer excavated units than the hillside sites (30 and 25 units), the number of units dug says nothing about how densely pottery was discarded. This comparison does not use the number of sherds at all.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The hillside sites do have more sherds in total (840 + 650 = 1,490) than the terrace sites (480 + 700 = 1,180), but they also had more excavated units (55 versus 32). Comparing raw totals ignores the unequal digging effort, and this comparison would not support the hypothesis.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Alder Flat recovered 480 sherds, which is fewer than the 650 recovered at Dunmore Ridge, so it is not true that both river terrace sites recovered more sherds. A comparison of raw totals would also fail to account for the different numbers of units excavated.

question_text:
Agronomist Teodoro Villanueva tested two lots of winter wheat seed to advise small farms on which supplier to buy from. He planted every seed in each lot in identical trays under the same greenhouse conditions and recorded how many seeds germinated within 14 days. He concluded that the lot from Pell Cooperative was the more reliable of the two, even though the lot from Harbin Farm produced more germinated seeds overall.

Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Villanueva's conclusion?
answer_a: The Harbin Farm lot had more germinated seeds than the Pell Cooperative lot, so a seed from the Harbin Farm lot was more likely to germinate.
answer_b: Both lots had more seeds that germinated than seeds that did not, so the two lots germinated at essentially the same rate.
answer_c: A larger share of the seeds in the Pell Cooperative lot germinated than of the seeds in the Harbin Farm lot, even though fewer Pell Cooperative seeds germinated in total.
answer_d: The Harbin Farm lot had more than twice as many germinated seeds as the Pell Cooperative lot, so it germinated at more than twice the rate.
explanation: Villanueva's conclusion is about reliability, meaning how likely a seed from each lot is to germinate. Because the lots contain different numbers of seeds, this must be judged by the share of each lot that germinated, not by the raw counts of germinated seeds. Dividing each lot's germinated seeds by its total shows that a larger share of Pell Cooperative seeds germinated than of Harbin Farm seeds, even though Harbin Farm's lot had more germinated seeds because it was much larger. Choice C states this comparison and so supports the conclusion.
distractor_a_explanation: The counts are accurate (Harbin Farm had more germinated seeds), but the lots are different sizes, so a larger count does not mean a higher germination rate. Harbin Farm's lot was much larger, which explains its higher count. Comparing proportions reverses the conclusion.
distractor_b_explanation: It is true that germinated seeds outnumbered non-germinated seeds in both lots, but that does not show the rates are equal. The share that germinated is noticeably higher for Pell Cooperative, so this contradicts, rather than supports, Villanueva's conclusion.
distractor_d_explanation: The count comparison is accurate, but it confuses a ratio of counts with a ratio of rates. Harbin Farm's lot was more than twice the size of Pell Cooperative's, so its larger count says nothing about a doubled rate; its germination share is actually lower.

question_text:
When the city of Danforth Heights launched a curbside composting pilot in 2019, many residents doubted that enough households would sign up to justify the expense. Over the next four years, the program's coordinator tracked enrollment, the amount of food waste collected, and the number of pickup routes. After reviewing the figures, the coordinator concluded that the program's enrollment grew by a larger percentage during one particular one-year interval than during any of the others.

Which choice best describes data from the table that support the coordinator's conclusion?
answer_a: Enrollment increased from 500 households in 2019 to 600 households in 2020.
answer_b: Enrollment increased from 600 households in 2020 to 840 households in 2021.
answer_c: Enrollment increased from 840 households in 2021 to 1,092 households in 2022.
answer_d: Enrollment increased from 1,092 households in 2022 to 1,365 households in 2023.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it identifies the interval in which enrollment grew by the largest percentage. Comparing each one-year increase with the enrollment at the start of that interval gives 20% for 2019 to 2020 (100 of 500), 40% for 2020 to 2021 (240 of 600), 30% for 2021 to 2022 (252 of 840), and 25% for 2022 to 2023 (273 of 1,092). The 40% increase from 2020 to 2021 is the largest, so the data for that interval support the coordinator's conclusion.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. This interval had the smallest increase in households of any interval (100), and its percentage increase (20%) is also smaller than that of the 2020 to 2021 interval (40%).
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. Enrollment rose by 252 households in this interval, which is 30% of the 2021 enrollment, a smaller percentage than the 40% increase from 2020 to 2021.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. This is the interval with the greatest increase in the number of households (273), but it started from the largest enrollment in the table, so the percentage increase (25%) is smaller than the 40% increase from 2020 to 2021.

question_text:
A conservation biologist surveying remnant patches of native prairie recorded the area of each patch and the number of native plant species found in it. The biologist expected larger patches to hold more species and fitted a line to the data to show that general trend. The scatterplot shows the eight patches surveyed, each labeled by name, along with the fitted line.

The biologist claims that one patch has been especially well preserved, supporting more native plant species than its size alone would lead one to anticipate.

Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the biologist's claim?
answer_a: Dunmore, because its point lies above the fitted line, showing more species than predicted for its size.
answer_b: Fennel Bank, because its point sits at a greater vertical distance above the fitted line than any other patch's point does.
answer_c: Harrow Green, because its point is higher on the graph than any other patch's point, showing the most species surveyed.
answer_d: Ironwood, because it is the largest patch surveyed, and larger patches tend to hold more native plant species.
explanation: Choice B is the best answer because the claim concerns a patch with more species than its area would predict, and the fitted line represents that prediction. The patch whose point is farthest above the line is therefore the one that most exceeds the trend for its size. Of the eight points, Fennel Bank's is separated from the line by the greatest vertical distance above it.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. Dunmore's point does lie above the fitted line, but only by a small margin, and another patch's point lies much farther above the line. Being above the line is not enough to support the claim of the most exceptional patch.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. This choice uses the raw species count: Harrow Green's point is the highest on the graph, but it is also a large patch, so a high count is largely what the line already predicts for its size. Its point is above the line by a smaller margin than Fennel Bank's.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. Ironwood is the largest patch, but its point falls slightly below the fitted line, meaning it has fewer species than expected for its size. Its size explains its high count rather than supporting the claim.

visual_data.title: Native plant species by prairie patch area
